newsitem.title: UK: EMU honeymoon may be unsafe for marriage - report.
newsitem.headline: EMU honeymoon may be unsafe for marriage - report.

text.p: Europe's transition towards a single currency faces serious pitfalls unless coherent measures for setting the eventual currency conversion rates are implemented soon, a report published by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) said.

CEPR said on Friday the transition period for European Monetary Union (EMU) - which stretches from the time when EMU "ins" are selected in Spring 1998 to when EMU is scheduled to start on January 1, 1999 - will create problems which may encourage adverse market speculation.

"To avoid these pitfalls we propose to pre-announce the bilateral conversion rates for the ins and then rely on floating to proceed to these fixed end-points," CEPR said in its report, "EMU: Getting the end game right."
Provided the conversion rates are credible, market rates will steadily converge to them without the need for any intervention ecven if EMU remains some way off.
"Complete credibility of bilateral conversion rates requires, if necessary, the prospect of substantial intervention on the final day to enforce these rates," said the report.

The CEPR report said pre-announced conversion rates between ins should be based on their central exchange rates in the existing European exchange rate mechanism and announced when when the candidates are first confirmed.

Pre-ins, country's who do not start in the first wave but aspire to join shortly after, should be required to join at exchange rates, relative to the new euro, based on their central parities in the revamped post-EMU ERM. These rates should be confirmed at the time their EMU membership is accepted.
The Maastricht Treaty requirement of no devaluation for two years prior to EMU entry would remain in force, they argued.
"This entire procedure should be announced as soon as possible. Speculative crises, typically, do not wait for policy decisions to be made," said CERP.
Unless measures are taken, CEPR said the interim period could become a time of increased exchange rate speculation, destabilising the exchange rates of the countries selected to participate in EMU.
The delicate interim period could open a window for playing 'end-games' of frivolous monetary and fiscal policies that could further destabilise exchange rates, said the report.
"An orgiastic honeymoon is not the safest route to lasting marriage," said the report.

CEPR said the institutional mechanisms for assuring a smooth convergence to EMU, such as the requirement to fulfil the debt and deficit rules, will have no more bite once the list of members has been revealed and may lead to some last-minute attempts at economic stimulation.
At the same time the Stability Pact, designed to keep economies converged after they join EMU, will not yet be in place and could encourage governments to manipulate exchange rates, the report said.

"Any coherent proposal for managing the transition must deal with two difficulties: Beliefs about eventual conversion rates may be self-fulfilling; and ins may be tempted to play end-games, relaxing previous austerity once their selection for EMU is irreversible," CEPR said.

Most existing proposals, said the report, fail to confront these challenges as do other flawed proposals include narrowing the ERM bands or conversion rates based on historical averages of actual exchange rates.

The report said while it might be argued that the risk of exchange market instability during the interim period could be mitigated, and national economic policy disciplined, by returning to narrow EMS bands, experience has taught its disciplining effect was quite limited.
"More importantly, the ERM crisis of 1992/93 has demonstrated forcefully how vulnerable narrow exchange rate bands are to speculative attacks."
